Sharp effective Nullstellensatz for projective Cohen-Macaulay schemes

Zhi Li Address: Zhi Li: School of Mathematical Sciences and Key Laboratory of Mathematics and Information Networks (Ministry of Education), Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing 100876, China. Email address: lizhi@amss.ac.cn , Xiankui Meng Address: Xiankui Meng: School of Mathematical Sciences and Key Laboratory of Mathematics and Information Networks (Ministry of Education), Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing 100876, China. Email address: mengxiankui@amss.ac.cn , Xiaoyu Su Address: Xiaoyu Su: School of Mathematical Sciences and Key Laboratory of Mathematics and Information Networks (Ministry of Education), Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications, Beijing 100876, China. Email address: xiaoyusu@bupt.edu.cn and Langfeng Zhu Address: Langfeng Zhu: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Wuhan University, Wuhan 430072, China Email address: zhulangfeng@amss.ac.cn
Abstract.

In this paper, we prove a sharp effective Nullstellensatz for projective Cohen-Macaulay schemes of pure dimension over an arbitrary field. In particular, if LL is an ample line bundle on a smooth complex projective variety XX and 𝒥⊆𝒪X\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{X} is a coherent ideal sheaf with 𝒥⊗L\mathcal{J}\otimes L globally generated, then (𝒥)degL⁡X⊆𝒥(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{L}X}\subseteq\mathcal{J}. This establishes the sharp bound conjectured by Ein and Lazarsfeld. More generally, we obtain sharp bounds in terms of mixed intersection numbers and a refinement involving products of powers of prime ideal sheaves associated to the irreducible components of the base locus. We also establish sharp radical power bounds for homogeneous ideals in finitely generated standard graded Cohen-Macaulay domains, extending Kollár’s sharp effective Nullstellensatz for polynomial rings. The proofs combine purity and cycle preservation for leading Ext sheaves with Koszul evaluation maps compatible with successive divisor cuts.

Key words and phrases: 
effective Nullstellensatz, divisor reduction, Cohen-Macaulay scheme, Noether exponent, Koszul complex, relative duality
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 14Q20; Secondary 13H10, 13D07, 14C17

1. Introduction

For an ideal I⊆ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]I\subseteq\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}], Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz states that the vanishing ideal of the zero locus defined by II equals the radical of II. In other words, if a polynomial ff vanishes on the zero locus of II, then f∈If\in\sqrt{I}, which means fm∈If^{m}\in I for some sufficiently large mm. The effective version of the Nullstellensatz makes Hilbert’s Nullstellensatz quantitative by giving explicit upper bounds for the exponent mm. This question was first considered by Hermann [7], and a major breakthrough was achieved by Brownawell [3]. For polynomial rings, sharp bounds were obtained by Kollár [10] and Jelonek [9] over an arbitrary field, including bounds for powers of homogeneous radicals as well. In [5], Ein and Lazarsfeld formulated an effective Nullstellensatz in the setting of smooth complex projective varieties. For further developments and variants of the effective Nullstellensatz, we refer the reader to [14, 15, 16, 4, 17, 11, 1].

This work is motivated by the results of Kollár [10] and Ein-Lazarsfeld [5]. Kollár proved sharp effective Nullstellensatz bounds for polynomial rings over arbitrary fields, including estimates for ordinary powers of homogeneous radicals. In particular, on ℙn\mathbb{P}^{n} with n≥2n\geq 2, for ideals generated by homogeneous polynomials of common degree a≥3a\geq 3, his result yields the exponent ana^{n}. Subsequently, Ein and Lazarsfeld considered the effective Nullstellensatz bounds in the setting of smooth complex projective varieties: for an ample line bundle LL over an nn-dimensional smooth projective variety XX, and for an ideal sheaf 𝒥\mathcal{J} with 𝒥⊗L\mathcal{J}\otimes L globally generated, they established

(𝒥)n​degL​X⊆𝒥.(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{n\deg_{L}X}\subseteq\mathcal{J}.

However, they suggested that the exponent n​degL​Xn\deg_{L}X may be sharpened to degL⁡X\deg_{L}X.

Conjecture 1.1 (Ein-Lazarsfeld [5]).

If XX is a smooth complex projective variety, LL is an ample line bundle, 𝒥\mathcal{J} is an ideal sheaf with 𝒥⊗L\mathcal{J}\otimes L globally generated, then

(𝒥)degL⁡X⊆𝒥.(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{L}X}\subseteq\mathcal{J}.

The very ample case of this conjecture was proved by Jelonek [9].

In this paper, we prove Conjecture 1.1 in full generality by establishing the following theorem in a general framework.

Let XX be a projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension nn over a field kk, and 𝒥⊆𝒪X\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{X} a coherent ideal sheaf.   2. (2)

    Br∖|B|=∅B_{r}\setminus|B|=\varnothing if r<nr<n.

Moreover, there exist finitely many irreducible closed subsets Wα⊆|B|W_{\alpha}\subseteq|B|, endowed with their reduced subscheme structures, and positive integers mαm_{\alpha}, such that ⋃α|Wα|=|B|\bigcup_{\alpha}|W_{\alpha}|=|B|,

As an application of Theorem 1.2, we can obtain the following consequence by choosing suitable linear combinations of the generating sections.

Corollary 1.3.

Let XX be a projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension nn over a field kk. Let LL be an ample line bundle such that 𝒥⊗L\mathcal{J}\otimes L is globally generated by mm sections. For any ample line bundle AA, one has (𝒥)d⊆𝒥(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{d}\subseteq\mathcal{J} for

d={deg⁡(c1​(L)m​c1​(A)n−m∩[X]),m<n;deg⁡(c1​(L)n∩[X]),m≥n.d=\begin{cases}\deg(c_{1}(L)^{m}c_{1}(A)^{n-m}\cap[X]),&m<n;\\ \deg(c_{1}(L)^{n}\cap[X]),&m\geq n.\end{cases}

In particular, if L=AaL=A^{a} with a≥1a\geq 1, then (𝒥)degA⁡X⋅amin⁡{m,n}⊆𝒥(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{A}X\cdot a^{\min\{m,n\}}}\subseteq\mathcal{J}.

By taking A=LA=L, Corollary 1.3 yields the following result with a sharp bound, which gives an affirmative answer to Conjecture 1.1.

Corollary 1.4.

Let XX be a projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension nn over a field kk. If LL is ample and 𝒥⊗L\mathcal{J}\otimes L is globally generated, then

(𝒥)degL⁡X⊆𝒥.(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{L}X}\subseteq\mathcal{J}.

Applying Theorem 1.2 with suitable powers of an ample line bundle LL, we obtain the following bounds in terms of the powers of LL and the degree of the variety with respect to LL.

Corollary 1.5.

Let XX be an integral projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of dimension nn over a field kk. Let LL be an ample and globally generated line bundle, and let fi∈H0​(X,Lai)f_{i}\in H^{0}(X,L^{a_{i}}) be nonzero sections with a1≥⋯≥am≥1a_{1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{m}\geq 1, which generate 𝒥\mathcal{J}. Then one has (𝒥)d⊆𝒥(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{d}\subseteq\mathcal{J} for

d={degLX⋅a1⋯am,m≤n;degLX⋅a1⋯an−1am,m>n>1;degL⁡X⋅am,n=1.d=\begin{cases}\deg_{L}X\cdot a_{1}\cdots a_{m},&m\leq n;\\ \deg_{L}X\cdot a_{1}\cdots a_{n-1}a_{m},&m>n>1;\\ \deg_{L}X\cdot a_{m},&n=1.\end{cases}

The exponents in the preceding three corollaries are sharp. Indeed, Example 4.3 realizes the bound in Corollary 1.5, taking all degrees equal shows that the bound in Corollary 1.3 is sharp, and taking them all equal to one attains the exponent degL⁡X\deg_{L}X in Corollary 1.4. We also note that the Cohen-Macaulay hypothesis is essential for these sharp bounds, see Example 4.4.

For X=ℙnX=\mathbb{P}^{n}, L=𝒪ℙn​(1)L=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{n}}(1), n≥2n\geq 2, and ai≥3a_{i}\geq 3, the exponent in Corollary 1.5 agrees with Kollár’s bound for homogeneous ideals [10, Theorem 1.5]. Kollár’s conclusion also controls the original homogeneous ideal at the vertex of the affine cone. For n=1n=1 and m>1m>1, the respective exponents are ama_{m} for the ideal-sheaf assertion and a1+am−1a_{1}+a_{m}-1 for the homogeneous ideal assertion.

On a projective scheme, containment of ideal sheaves does not alone imply containment in the original homogeneous ideal: one must also control the contribution at the vertex of the affine cone. Our second main theorem supplies this additional, control which gives the optimal exponent under the Cohen-Macaulay hypothesis.

Theorem 1.6.

Let S=⨁ν=0∞SνS=\bigoplus_{\nu=0}^{\infty}S_{\nu} be a finitely generated standard graded Cohen-Macaulay domain over a field kk, with S0=kS_{0}=k. Denote Y=Proj⁡SY=\operatorname{Proj}S and n=dimS−1≥1n=\dim S-1\geq 1. Let I=(f1,…,fm)I=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}), where the fif_{i} are homogeneous elements of degrees a1≥⋯≥am≥1a_{1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{m}\geq 1. Set

d=max{deg𝒪⁡(1)Y⋅ama1⋯amin⁡{m,n}−1,deg𝒪⁡(1)Y−1+am+∑i=1min⁡{m−1,n}(ai−1)}.d=\max\left\{\deg_{\mathcal{O}(1)}Y\cdot a_{m}a_{1}\cdots a_{\min\{m,n\}-1},\ \deg_{\mathcal{O}(1)}Y-1+a_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{\min\{m-1,n\}}(a_{i}-1)\right\}.

Then (I)d⊆I(\sqrt{I})^{d}\subseteq I.

For S=k⁡[x0,…,xn]S=k[x_{0},\ldots,x_{n}], Theorem 1.6 recovers Kollár’s bound [10, Theorem 1.5] without the assumption that every generator has degree at least 33. Jelonek [9] establishes effective bounds for homogeneous ideal containment without requiring the homogeneous coordinate ring to be Cohen-Macaulay. Jelonek’s bound is optimal when m≤nm\leq n, whereas for m>nm>n, Kollár’s theorem [10, Theorem 1.5] permits a slightly smaller exponent. The Cohen-Macaulay setting also appears in Sombra’s work [17, Theorem 1.8].

The first term in the expression for dd in Theorem 1.6 is the bound that already controls the projective ideal-sheaf inclusion. The second term accounts for the additional graded obstruction that corresponds to the term a1+am−1a_{1}+a_{m}-1 in [10, Theorem 1.5]. Both terms are necessary as Example 5.3 shows.

By homogenizing the polynomial functions on affine varieties, we obtain the following affine corollary from the preceding projective and graded bounds.

Corollary 1.7.

Let V⊆𝐀kNV\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{N}_{k} be an integral affine variety of dimension n≥1n\geq 1, and let Y⊆ℙkNY\subseteq\mathbb{P}^{N}_{k} be its projective closure. If 𝔞=k⁡[V]\mathfrak{a}=k[V], then there exist gi∈k⁡[V]g_{i}\in k[V] satisfying

(1.1) 1=∑i=1mgi​fi,deg⁡gi+ai≤d,1=\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_{i}f_{i},\quad\deg g_{i}+a_{i}\leq d,

where

d=max{degV⋅ama1⋯amin⁡{m,n}−1,degV−1+am+∑i=1min⁡{m−1,n}(ai−1)}.d=\max\left\{\deg V\cdot a_{m}a_{1}\cdots a_{\min\{m,n\}-1},\ \deg V-1+a_{m}+\sum_{i=1}^{\min\{m-1,n\}}(a_{i}-1)\right\}.

In particular, the conclusion holds if kk is algebraically closed and the fif_{i} have no common zero.

The degree of a function in k⁡[V]k[V] is the smallest total degree of any polynomial representing it on VV, relative to the given embedding V⊆𝐀kNV\subseteq\mathbf{A}^{N}_{k}. The estimate (1.1) controls the degree of each gig_{i} and implies deg⁡(gi​fi)≤d\deg(g_{i}f_{i})\leq d. On a general affine variety, deg⁡(gi​fi)\deg(g_{i}f_{i}) and deg⁡gi+ai\deg g_{i}+a_{i} are different in general. For example, in k⁡[x,t]/(x​tδ−1−1)k[x,t]/(xt^{\delta-1}-1) with δ≥2\delta\geq 2, the functions f=xaf=x^{a} and g=t(δ−1)​ag=t^{(\delta-1)a} satisfy deg⁡f+deg⁡g=a⋅deg⁡Y\deg f+\deg g=a\cdot\deg Y but f​g=1fg=1. Thus the product has degree 00, while the sum of the degrees can be large.

Our proofs of Theorem 1.2 and Theorem 1.6 use a homological approach based on duality and Koszul evaluation maps. This differs from the use of the Skoda-type division theorem in Ein-Lazarsfeld [5], and from the elimination methods of Jelonek [9]. We develop the successive cutting and degree-counting strategy of [10] by combining pure leading Ext sheaves with compatible Koszul evaluation images. The purity and cycle properties of the leading Ext sheaves are classical facts [13, 18]. Their role here is as follows: at each step of removing |B||B|-torsion, they convert the degree of the removed top-dimensional cycle into an annihilator, which can then be transported to the next cut.

Section 2 introduces the cycles, duality, and evaluation-images. Section 3 proves Theorem 1.2. Section 4 presents the proofs of Corollary 1.3 and Corollary 1.5, and gives sharpness examples. Finally, Section 5 proves Theorem 1.6 and Corollary 1.7, and provides sharpness examples.

2. Cycles, leading Ext, and evaluation images

This section collects some facts used in the proof of the main theorems. We first recall associated cycles and mixed intersection degrees. Using generic lengths, we obtain bounds for annihilators of pure sheaves. Then we apply local Grothendieck duality with the dualizing sheaf to establish purity and cycle preservation for leading Ext sheaves on Cohen-Macaulay schemes. Finally, we introduce the notion of the evaluation image ideal. Using Koszul complexes and relative duality maps, we construct a morphism from the leading Ext sheaves to the structure sheaf 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B} of the base scheme, whose image is precisely the evaluation-image ideal. This construction allows our inductive argument to proceed, and translates annihilation statements for Ext sheaves into ideal-power containments in 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B}.

2.1. Cycles and mixed intersection degrees

We now recall the cycle-theoretic formalism which provides the quantitative degree estimates underlying the inductive bound. We begin with the cycle associated to a coherent sheaf, the notion of purity, and the intersection identities used throughout the proof.

Definition 2.1 ([6] Example 15.1.8, [18] Tag 02QX).

Let XX be a projective scheme over a field kk, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a coherent sheaf with dimSupp⁡ℳ≤q\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}\leq q. Its associated qq-cycle is

[ℳ]q:=∑dim{η}¯=qLength𝒪X,η⁡(ℳη)​[{η}¯].[\mathcal{M}]_{q}:=\sum_{\dim\overline{\{\eta\}}=q}\operatorname{Length}_{\mathcal{O}_{X,\eta}}(\mathcal{M}_{\eta})[\overline{\{\eta\}}].

The sum runs over the generic points of the qq-dimensional irreducible components of Supp⁡ℳ\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}, each endowed with its reduced structure. For a closed subscheme Z⊆XZ\subseteq X, we write [Z]q=[𝒪Z]q[Z]_{q}=[\mathcal{O}_{Z}]_{q}. We use the same notation for these cycles and their classes in the Chow group CHq⁡(X)\operatorname{CH}_{q}(X).

[ℳ]q[\mathcal{M}]_{q} is effective, and it is zero if dimSupp⁡ℳ<q\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}<q. It follows from [6, Proposition 2.5] that, for an invertible sheaf LL, the intersection with its first Chern class defines an operator c1​(L)∩−:CHq⁡(X)→CHq−1⁡(X)c_{1}(L)\cap-:\operatorname{CH}_{q}(X)\rightarrow\operatorname{CH}_{q-1}(X). These operators commute and are additive with respect to tensor products of invertible sheaves. We use their products to form intersection numbers

deg(c1(L1)⋯c1(Lq)∩[ℳ]q).\deg\bigl(c_{1}(L_{1})\cdots c_{1}(L_{q})\cap[\mathcal{M}]_{q}\bigr).

Here deg\deg denotes the degree of a zero-cycle, with deg[x]=[κ(x):k]\deg[x]=[\kappa(x):k] for a closed point xx. When q=0q=0, the product of Chern classes is understood to be empty. These constructions apply to singular and nonreduced schemes, see [6, Chapters 1–2]. The usual degree of XX with respect to an ample line bundle LL is degL⁡X=deg⁡(c1​(L)dimX∩[X]dimX)\deg_{L}X=\deg\bigl(c_{1}(L)^{\dim X}\cap[X]_{\dim X}\bigr).

We collect some basic properties of cycles and intersection numbers, which form the basis for the degree estimates in our induction.

Proposition 2.2.

Let XX be a projective scheme over a field kk, and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a coherent sheaf with dimSupp⁡ℳ≤q\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}\leq q.

    For an exact sequence 0→ℳ′→ℳ→𝒬→00\to\mathcal{M}^{\prime}\to\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{Q}\to 0, one has [ℳ]q=[ℳ′]q+[𝒬]q[\mathcal{M}]_{q}=[\mathcal{M}^{\prime}]_{q}+[\mathcal{Q}]_{q} as cycles on XX.

    In particular, over an algebraically closed field, this degree is the total length of ℳ\mathcal{M}.

  • (3)

    If AA is an invertible sheaf, then [ℳ⊗A]q=[ℳ]q[\mathcal{M}\otimes A]_{q}=[\mathcal{M}]_{q}.

  • (4)

    Suppose q≥1q\geq 1, and let LL be an invertible sheaf with a section s∈H0​(X,L)s\in H^{0}(X,L) such that multiplication by ss induces an injection ℳ⊗L−1→𝑠ℳ\mathcal{M}\otimes L^{-1}\xrightarrow{s}\mathcal{M}. Denote H=V⁡(s)H=V(s) and regard ℳ|H\mathcal{M}|_{H} as a sheaf on XX. Then

    dimSupp⁡(ℳ|H)≤q−1,[ℳ|H]q−1=c1​(L)∩[ℳ]q\dim\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal{M}|_{H})\leq q-1,\quad[\mathcal{M}|_{H}]_{q-1}=c_{1}(L)\cap[\mathcal{M}]_{q}

    in CHq−1⁡(X)\operatorname{CH}_{q-1}(X). Consequently, for line bundles L1,…,Lq−1L_{1},\ldots,L_{q-1},

    deg(c1(L1)⋯c1(Lq−1)∩[ℳ|H]q−1)=deg(c1(L1)⋯c1(Lq−1)c1(L)∩[ℳ]q).\deg\bigl(c_{1}(L_{1})\cdots c_{1}(L_{q-1})\cap[\mathcal{M}|_{H}]_{q-1}\bigr)=\deg\bigl(c_{1}(L_{1})\cdots c_{1}(L_{q-1})c_{1}(L)\cap[\mathcal{M}]_{q}\bigr).
Proof.

Assertions (1) and (3) follow from the definition of associated cycles and additivity of length [18, Tags 02QX and 02QZ]. Assertion (2) follows from linearity, the definition of degree, and positivity of ample intersections [18, Tag 0BEV]. Finally, (4) follows from the local length formula for a regular section and its interpretation as intersection with the first Chern class [18, Tags 02QG and 02SN]. The intersection degree formula followed by intersection with the remaining Chern classes. ∎

A coherent sheaf is pure of dimension qq (cf. [8, Definition 1.1.2] and [12, p. 49]) if every nonzero coherent subsheaf has support dimension qq, equivalently, all its associated points are generic points of qq-dimensional support components. The following lemma gives multiplicity bounds for annihilators.

Lemma 2.3.

Let 𝒥⊆𝒪X{\mathcal{J}}\subseteq{\mathcal{O}}_{X} be a coherent ideal sheaf, and let L1,…,LqL_{1},\ldots,L_{q} be ample line bundles. If the coherent sheaf ℳ\mathcal{M} is zero or pure of dimension qq, and if Supp⁡ℳ⊆|V⁡(𝒥)|\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}\subseteq|V({\mathcal{J}})|, then

(𝒥)deg(c1(L1)⋯c1(Lq)∩[ℳ]q)ℳ=0.(\sqrt{{\mathcal{J}}})^{\deg\left(c_{1}(L_{1})\cdots c_{1}(L_{q})\cap[\mathcal{M}]_{q}\right)}\mathcal{M}=0.

For 𝒢\mathcal{G} with dim𝒢=0\dim\mathcal{G}=0, we apply the same finite-length argument at each support point of 𝒢/𝒥​𝒢\mathcal{G}/{\mathcal{J}}\mathcal{G}. This quotient is supported on V⁡(𝒥)V({\mathcal{J}}), and Proposition 2.2 (1)–(2) gives Length𝒪X,x⁡((𝒢/𝒥​𝒢)x)≤deg⁡[𝒢/𝒥​𝒢]0≤deg⁡[𝒢]0\operatorname{Length}_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X,x}}\bigl((\mathcal{G}/{\mathcal{J}}\mathcal{G})_{x}\bigr)\leq\deg[\mathcal{G}/{\mathcal{J}}\mathcal{G}]_{0}\leq\deg[\mathcal{G}]_{0}. Thus (𝒥)deg⁡[𝒢]0(\sqrt{{\mathcal{J}}})^{\deg[\mathcal{G}]_{0}} annihilates 𝒢/𝒥​𝒢\mathcal{G}/{\mathcal{J}}\mathcal{G}, which proves the second assertion. ∎

2.2. Purity and cycle preservation of leading Ext

To prove the first assertion 𝒥d⊆𝒥\sqrt{\mathcal{J}}^{d}\subseteq\mathcal{J} in Theorem 1.2, it suffices to show (𝒥)d⋅𝒪B=0(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{d}\cdot\mathcal{O}_{B}=0, where B=V⁡(𝒥)B=V(\mathcal{J}) is the base scheme. Lemma 2.3 shows that generic multiplicities control annihilators once the sheaf is pure. To use this observation for the intermediate quotients in our induction, we therefore seek an operation that produces a pure sheaf while preserving its top-dimensional cycle. Local Grothendieck duality suggests such an operation.

Let XX be a projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension nn over kk. Then its dualizing complex is concentrated in degree −n-n and of the form ωX​[n]\omega_{X}[n] with ωX\omega_{X} a maximal Cohen-Macaulay coherent sheaf on XX. We call ωX\omega_{X} its dualizing sheaf. Moreover, the natural homothety morphism gives R​ℋ​o​mX​(ωX,ωX)≅𝒪XR\mathcal{H}om_{X}(\omega_{X},\omega_{X})\cong\mathcal{O}_{X}. See [18, Tags 0A7B, 0AWS, and 0FVU]. Recall that, for a closed immersion i:Z↪Xi:Z\hookrightarrow X, the right adjoint i!i^{!} produces the dualizing complex i!(ωX[n])i^{!}(\omega_{X}[n]) of ZZ. Its pushforward is computed by i∗i!(ωX[n])≅RℋomX(i∗𝒪Z,ωX[n])i_{*}i^{!}(\omega_{X}[n])\cong R\mathcal{H}om_{X}(i_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Z},\omega_{X}[n]). This brings Ext sheaves into the picture as the cohomology sheaves of a dualizing complex. For a general coherent sheaf ℳ\mathcal{M} on XX, we use the analogous derived dual R​ℋ​o​mX​(ℳ,ωX​[n])R\mathcal{H}om_{X}(\mathcal{M},\omega_{X}[n]). If dimSupp⁡ℳ=q\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}=q, local duality gives vanishing below degree −q-q, so truncation isolates the leading Ext sheaf:

τ≤−q​R​ℋ​o​mX​(ℳ,ωX​[n])≅ℰ​x​tXn−q​(ℳ,ωX)​[q].\tau^{\leq-q}R\mathcal{H}om_{X}(\mathcal{M},\omega_{X}[n])\cong\mathcal{E}\!xt_{X}^{n-q}(\mathcal{M},\omega_{X})[q].

The significance of this leading term is that it is pure of dimension qq, even when ℳ\mathcal{M} is not Cohen-Macaulay, and preserves the associated qq-cycle. We therefore retain ωX\omega_{X} as the coefficient sheaf. Tensoring the resulting Ext sheaf with a line bundle preserves both properties. The following lemma records the statements we need.

Lemma 2.4.

Let XX be a projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension nn over a field kk with dualizing sheaf ωX\omega_{X}, and let 0≤q≤n0\leq q\leq n. For a coherent sheaf ℳ\mathcal{M} with dimSupp⁡ℳ≤q\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}\leq q, the following hold:

  1. (1)

    ℰ​x​tXj​(ℳ,ωX)=0{\mathcal{E}\!xt}_{X}^{j}(\mathcal{M},{\omega}_{X})=0 for j<n−qj<n-q;

  2. (2)

    ℰ​x​tXn−q​(ℳ,ωX){\mathcal{E}\!xt}_{X}^{n-q}(\mathcal{M},{\omega}_{X}) is zero or pure of dimension qq;

  3. (3)

    the equality of cycles [ℰ​x​tXn−q​(ℳ,ωX)]q=[ℳ]q[{\mathcal{E}\!xt}_{X}^{n-q}(\mathcal{M},{\omega}_{X})]_{q}=[\mathcal{M}]_{q} holds on XX.

If dimSupp⁡ℳ<q\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}<q, then ℰ​x​tXn−q​(ℳ,ωX)=0{\mathcal{E}\!xt}_{X}^{n-q}(\mathcal{M},{\omega}_{X})=0.

Proof.

The vanishing and purity assertions follow from the local canonical-module properties in [13, Theorem 1.8 and Lemma 1.9(c)]. The same vanishing gives the assertion when dimSupp⁡ℳ\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M} is less than qq. At the generic point η\eta of a qq-dimensional component of Supp⁡ℳ\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{M}, the ring 𝒪X,η{\mathcal{O}}_{X,\eta} is Cohen-Macaulay of dimension n−qn-q, and ℳη\mathcal{M}_{\eta} has finite length. Finite-length local duality [18, Tag 0A7Q] therefore gives

Length𝒪X,η⁡(ℰ​x​tXn−q​(ℳ,ωX)η)=Length𝒪X,η⁡(ℳη).\operatorname{Length}_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X,\eta}}\bigl({\mathcal{E}\!xt}_{X}^{n-q}(\mathcal{M},{\omega}_{X})_{\eta}\bigr)=\operatorname{Length}_{{\mathcal{O}}_{X,\eta}}(\mathcal{M}_{\eta}).

Since the Ext sheaf is supported on Supp⁡ℳ{\operatorname{Supp}}\mathcal{M}, these equalities give (3) by Definition 2.1. ∎

2.3. Evaluation image ideal

The evaluation image allows us to make comparisons between successive divisor cuts on the fixed base scheme B=V⁡(𝒥)B=V(\mathcal{J}). The sheaves supported on |B||B| will be controlled by Lemma 2.3, while the prescribed dimension conditions in Theorem 1.2 ensure that the next section is regular on the corresponding |B||B|-torsion-free quotient. Dual Koszul evaluations convert the resulting maps of Ext sheaves into maps of ideals in 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B}, through which annihilation statements pass from one stage to the next.

Throughout this subsection, let XX be a projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension nn over a field kk, and let 𝒥⊆𝒪X\mathcal{J}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{X} be a coherent ideal sheaf, with B=V⁡(𝒥)B=V(\mathcal{J}). Let L1,…,LrL_{1},\ldots,L_{r} be line bundles on XX, with 0≤r≤n0\leq r\leq n, and choose si∈H0​(X,𝒥⊗Li)s_{i}\in H^{0}(X,\mathcal{J}\otimes L_{i}). For 0≤j≤r0\leq j\leq r, write Bj=V⁡(s1,…,sj)=V⁡(s¯)B_{j}=V(s_{1},\ldots,s_{j})=V(\underline{s}) for their common zero scheme, B0=XB_{0}=X. Thus B⊆BjB\subseteq B_{j}. Each section sis_{i} gives a two-term complex [Li−1→si𝒪X]\left[L_{i}^{-1}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}\mathcal{O}_{X}\right] concentrated in degrees −1-1 and 00. Their total tensor product is the Koszul complex 𝖪(s¯)=𝖪(s1,…,sj)=Tot(⊗i=1j[Li−1→si𝒪X])\mathsf{K}(\underline{s})=\mathsf{K}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{j})=\operatorname{Tot}\left(\otimes_{i=1}^{j}\left[L_{i}^{-1}\xrightarrow{s_{i}}\mathcal{O}_{X}\right]\right), which takes the explicit form

0→⨂i=1jLi−1→⨁ℓ=1j⨂i≠ℓ1≤i≤jLi−1→⋯→⨁i=1jLi−1→(s1,…,sj)𝒪X→00\to\bigotimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}\to\bigoplus_{\ell=1}^{j}\bigotimes_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\neq\ell\\ 1\leq i\leq j\end{subarray}}L_{i}^{-1}\to\cdots\to\bigoplus_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}\xrightarrow{(s_{1},\dots,s_{j})}\mathcal{O}_{X}\to 0

The complex is concentrated in degrees −j,…,0-j,\ldots,0 and self dual under

R​ℋ​o​mX​(_,𝒪X)⊗i=1jLi−1​[j],R\mathcal{H}om_{X}(\_,\mathcal{O}_{X})\otimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}[j],

see [18, Tag 062J]. When the sections form a regular sequence, this complex resolves 𝒪Bj\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}. In general, one always has H0​(𝖪⁡(s1,…,sj))=𝒪Bj{H}^{0}\bigl(\mathsf{K}(s_{1},\ldots,s_{j})\bigr)=\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}.

Let ωX↠ℱ\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F} be a coherent quotient annihilated by s1,…,sjs_{1},\ldots,s_{j}, with dimSupp⁡ℱ≤n−j\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{F}\leq n-j. Tensoring the Koszul augmentation map 𝖪⁡(s¯)→𝒪Bj\mathsf{K}(\underline{s})\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}} with ωX\omega_{X} and composing with the induced quotient gives a chain map 𝖪⁡(s¯)⊗ωX→ωX⊗𝒪Bj↠ℱ\mathsf{K}(\underline{s})\otimes\omega_{X}\rightarrow\omega_{X}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}. We call this the augmentation of the quotient ωX↠ℱ\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}. Because the Koszul complex is locally free and self dual, the derived tensor-Hom adjunction gives

RℋomX(𝖪(s¯)⊗ωX,ωX)⊗i=1jLi−1[j]≅RℋomX(𝖪(s¯),⊗i=1jLi−1[j])≅𝖪(s¯).R\mathcal{H}om_{X}\bigl(\mathsf{K}(\underline{s})\otimes\omega_{X},\omega_{X}\bigr)\otimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}[j]\cong R\mathcal{H}om_{X}\bigl(\mathsf{K}(\underline{s}),\otimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}[j]\bigr)\cong\mathsf{K}(\underline{s}).

Dualizing the augmentation by R​ℋ​o​mX​(_,ωX⊗i=1jLi−1​[j])R\mathcal{H}om_{X}(\_,\omega_{X}\otimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}[j]), and taking cohomology in degree 00 therefore gives a natural evaluation map

evj:ℰ​x​tXj​(ℱ,ωX⊗i=1jLi−1)→𝒪Bj.\mathrm{ev}_{j}\colon\mathcal{E}\!xt_{X}^{j}(\mathcal{F},\omega_{X}\otimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1})\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}.

Its image is a coherent ideal sheaf of 𝒪Bj\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}. Taking its image under 𝒪Bj↠𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{B} leads to the following definition.

Definition 2.5.

The jj-th evaluation image ideal of the quotient ωX↠ℱ\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F} in 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B} is

𝔮j​(ℱ):=im⁡(ℰ​x​tXj​(ℱ,ωX)⊗i=1jLi−1→evj𝒪Bj↠𝒪B).\mathfrak{q}_{j}(\mathcal{F}):=\operatorname{im}\left(\mathcal{E}\!xt_{X}^{j}(\mathcal{F},\omega_{X})\otimes_{i=1}^{j}L_{i}^{-1}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{ev}_{j}}\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{B}\right).

For j=0j=0, the empty Koszul complex and the empty tensor product are both 𝒪X\mathcal{O}_{X}. In particular, 𝔮0​(ωX)=𝒪B\mathfrak{q}_{0}(\omega_{X})=\mathcal{O}_{B}.

The definition does not require the sections s1,…,sjs_{1},\ldots,s_{j} to form a regular sequence.

Remark 2.6.

Locally, assume in addition that XX is Gorenstein, the evaluation ideal 𝔮j​(ωX|Z)\mathfrak{q}_{j}(\omega_{X}|_{Z}) for closed subscheme Z⊆BjZ\subseteq B_{j} is the image in 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B} of the Koszul-Fitting ideal KittR⁡(s¯,IZ)\operatorname{Kitt}_{R}(\underline{s},I_{Z}) after trivializing the line bundles, see [2].

We now collect the basic properties of these evaluation image ideals.

Lemma 2.7.

Under the preceding hypotheses, let ωX↠ℱ\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F} be a quotient with

dimSupp⁡ℱ≤n−j.\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{F}\leq n-j.
  1. (1)

    The evaluation image ideal 𝔮j​(ℱ)\mathfrak{q}_{j}(\mathcal{F}) is coherent and supported on Supp⁡(ℱ)∩|B|\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal{F})\cap|B|. Its construction commutes with restriction to open subsets of XX.

  2. (2)

    For a further quotient ωX→ℱ↠ℱ′\omega_{X}\to\mathcal{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}^{\prime}, one has 𝔮j​(ℱ′)⊆𝔮j​(ℱ)\mathfrak{q}_{j}(\mathcal{F}^{\prime})\subseteq\mathfrak{q}_{j}(\mathcal{F}).

Proof.

Coherence follows since it is defined as the image of a morphism of coherent sheaves. The annihilator of ℱ\mathcal{F} annihilates ℰ​x​tXj​(ℱ,ωX)\mathcal{E}\!xt_{X}^{j}(\mathcal{F},\omega_{X}), and therefore annihilates its evaluation image as well. Since this image lies in 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B}, its support is contained in Supp⁡ℱ∩|B|\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{F}\cap|B|. The Koszul construction, derived duality, and the operation of taking images all commute with restriction to open subsets. This proves (1).

For (2), the augmentation to ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} factors as 𝖪⁡(s¯)⊗ωX→ℱ↠ℱ′\mathsf{K}(\underline{s})\otimes\omega_{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}^{\prime}. Contravariance of derived Hom therefore gives a morphism from the source of the evaluation for ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} to that for ℱ\mathcal{F}, compatible with their evaluation maps into 𝒪Bj\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}. Composing with 𝒪Bj↠𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{O}_{B} and taking images yields the desired inclusion. ∎

We next compare evaluation image ideals before and after restriction to the zero scheme of the next section. When this section is regular on the quotient sheaf being restricted, the evaluation images satisfy an inclusion in the fixed sheaf 𝒪B\mathcal{O}_{B}. This inclusion will allow us to pass from one stage of the induction to the next.

Lemma 2.8.

Let 0≤j<r0\leq j<r, and let ωX↠ℱ\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F} be a quotient as above. Suppose that sj+1s_{j+1} is regular on ℱ\mathcal{F}, and H=V⁡(sj+1)H=V(s_{j+1}). Regard ℱ|H\mathcal{F}|_{H} as a sheaf on XX, with its induced quotient map from ωX\omega_{X}. Then s1,…,sj+1s_{1},\ldots,s_{j+1} annihilate ℱ|H\mathcal{F}|_{H}, dimSupp⁡(ℱ|H)≤n−j−1\dim\operatorname{Supp}(\mathcal{F}|_{H})\leq n-j-1, and

(2.1) 𝔮j​(ℱ)⊆𝔮j+1​(ℱ|H).\mathfrak{q}_{j}(\mathcal{F})\subseteq\mathfrak{q}_{j+1}(\mathcal{F}|_{H}).
Proof.

Since the evaluation maps are obtained by applying derived duality to the Koszul augmentations, comparing their images requires us to understand how these augmentations interact with multiplication by sj+1s_{j+1} and the resulting cut. Write s¯=(s1,…,sj)\underline{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{j}), and consider the augmentation aug:𝖪⁡(s¯)⊗ωX→𝒪Bj⊗ωX↠ℱ\mathrm{aug}\colon\mathsf{K}(\underline{s})\otimes\omega_{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}\otimes\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}. On the Koszul side, adjoining sj+1s_{j+1} amounts to tensoring with the two-term complex 𝖪(sj+1)=[Lj+1−1→sj+1𝒪X]\mathsf{K}(s_{j+1})=[L_{j+1}^{-1}\xrightarrow{s_{j+1}}\mathcal{O}_{X}], or equivalently, taking the mapping cone of multiplication by sj+1s_{j+1}:

On ℱ\mathcal{F}, the same construction computes restriction to HH: regularity of sj+1s_{j+1} on ℱ\mathcal{F} gives the exact sequence 0→ℱ⊗Lj+1−1→sj+1ℱ→ℱ|H→00\to\mathcal{F}\otimes L_{j+1}^{-1}\xrightarrow{s_{j+1}}\mathcal{F}\rightarrow\mathcal{F}|_{H}\to 0 and also implies dimℱ|H≤n−j−1\dim\mathcal{F}|_{H}\leq n-j-1. The augmentation and quotient maps commute with multiplication by sj+1s_{j+1} at the level of complexes. The induced maps of mapping cones therefore fit into the following commutative diagram in the derived category:

Here the third column consists of morphisms in the derived category induced by the mapping cone construction, qj+1q_{j+1} is the quotient map from the Koszul complex, and qq is the quotient map given by the cone construction. Thus the augmentation maps induce a commutative diagram of distinguished triangles:

3. Proof of Theorem 1.2

We prove Theorem 1.2 by successively removing |B||B|-torsion and taking regular cuts of quotients of ωX\omega_{X}.

Proof of Theorem 1.2.

Let U=X∖|B|U=X\setminus|B|. Starting with ℱ0=ωX\mathcal{F}_{0}=\omega_{X}, we construct a sequence of coherent quotient sheaves ωX↠ℱ1↠⋯↠ℱr\omega_{X}\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}_{1}\twoheadrightarrow\cdots\twoheadrightarrow\mathcal{F}_{r} by removing the subsheaves of sections supported on |B||B| and then restricting to the zero scheme of the next prescribed section.

At the jj-th stage with 0≤j≤r0\leq j\leq r, we remove the |B||B|-torsion Γ|B|​ℱj\Gamma_{|B|}\mathcal{F}_{j} and define

ℱjB​tf=ℱj/Γ|B|​ℱj.\mathcal{F}_{j}^{B\mathrm{tf}}=\mathcal{F}_{j}/\Gamma_{|B|}\mathcal{F}_{j}.

Here the superscript B​tf{B\mathrm{tf}} denotes |B||B|-torsion-free quotient, obtained by quotienting ℱj\mathcal{F}_{j} by its 𝒥\mathcal{J}-torsion subsheaf Γ|B|​ℱj\Gamma_{|B|}\mathcal{F}_{j}. The subsheaf Γ|B|​ℱj\Gamma_{|B|}\mathcal{F}_{j} is coherent and supported on BB, and Ass⁡(ℱjB​tf)∩|B|=∅\operatorname{Ass}\bigl(\mathcal{F}_{j}^{B\mathrm{tf}}\bigr)\cap|B|=\varnothing. Suppose inductively that Supp⁡ℱj⊆Bj\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{F}_{j}\subseteq B_{j}, ℱj|U=ωX⊗𝒪Bj|U\mathcal{F}_{j}|_{U}=\omega_{X}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{B_{j}}|_{U}, and dimSupp⁡ℱj≤n−j\dim\operatorname{Supp}\mathcal{F}_{j}\leq n-j.

Indeed, on UU, the restriction of sj+1s_{j+1} is regular on ℱjB​tf|U\mathcal{F}_{j}^{B\mathrm{tf}}|_{U}. Thus sj+1s_{j+1} is regular on Bj|UB_{j}|_{U}, and its zero scheme is Cohen-Macaulay and pure of dimension n−j−1n-j-1. Hence sj+1s_{j+1} is regular on ℱjB​tf\mathcal{F}_{j}^{B\mathrm{tf}}.

4. Corollaries of Theorem 1.2

We now give some applications of Theorem 1.2 by choosing suitable line bundles and sections. This yields radical-power bounds for fewer generators and generators of unequal degrees. When the choice of auxiliary sections requires an infinite field, we pass to k⁡(t)k(t); the relevant intersection degrees are unchanged, and the resulting radical-power containments descend to kk by faithful flatness.

Proof of Corollary 1.3.

After replacing kk by k⁡(t)k(t) if necessary, we may assume that kk is infinite. Let f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} generate 𝒥⊗L\mathcal{J}\otimes L, and take B=V⁡(𝒥)B=V(\mathcal{J}). We can choose r=min⁡{m,n}r=\min\{m,n\} linear combinations

(s1,…,sr)=(f1,…,fm)​C(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r})=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})C

with C∈Mm×r​(k)C\in M_{m\times r}(k) of full rank, such that each successive section is regular on the preceding common zero scheme outside |B||B|. Indeed, at each associated point outside |B||B|, the generators f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} do not all vanish. Thus the vanishing of the next linear combination rules out a proper linear subspace of the coefficient space. The span of the preceding coefficient vectors is also proper. Avoiding these finitely many subspaces gives the required choice.

Since XX is Cohen-Macaulay and pure-dimensional, successive regular sections give dim(V⁡(s¯)∖|B|)≤n−j\dim\bigl(V(\underline{s})\setminus|B|\bigr)\leq n-j, 1≤j≤r1\leq j\leq r. If r=m<nr=m<n, the coefficient matrix is invertible, so the new sections generate the same ideal sheaf and V⁡(s1,…,sm)=BV(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})=B. Thus the condition (2) of Theorem 1.2 also holds. Apply Theorem 1.2 with L1=⋯=Lr=A=LL_{1}=\cdots=L_{r}=A=L. The last assertion follows from c1​(Aa)=a⋅c1​(A)c_{1}(A^{a})=a\cdot c_{1}(A). ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.5.

Let r=min⁡{m,n}r=\min\{m,n\} and B=V⁡(𝒥)B=V(\mathcal{J}). Take s1=fms_{1}=f_{m}, which is regular because XX is integral. For 1≤j<r1\leq j<r, choose successively

(4.1) sj+1=fj+∑i=j+1m−1uj​i​fi,uj​i∈H0​(X,Laj−ai).s_{j+1}=f_{j}+\sum_{i=j+1}^{m-1}u_{ji}f_{i},\quad u_{ji}\in H^{0}(X,L^{a_{j}-a_{i}}).

At any associated point of V⁡(s1,…,sj)V(s_{1},\ldots,s_{j}) outside |B||B|, the sections fj,…,fm−1f_{j},\ldots,f_{m-1} cannot all vanish: otherwise the preceding triangular equations, read backwards, would force all the fif_{i} to vanish at that point. Since each Laj−aiL^{a_{j}-a_{i}} is globally generated, the condition that sj+1s_{j+1} vanish at such a point is either empty or a proper affine linear condition. Avoiding the finitely many proper affine subspaces makes sj+1s_{j+1} regular on the preceding common zero scheme outside |B||B|. Hence all the dimension conditions of Theorem 1.2 hold.

If r=m<nr=m<n, then after local trivialization of LL, the full list (s1,…,sm)(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}) is obtained from (fm,f1,…,fm−1)(f_{m},f_{1},\ldots,f_{m-1}) by an invertible triangular change. Consequently, V⁡(s1,…,sm)=BV(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m})=B, which gives the condition (2) of Theorem 1.2. Take L1=LamL_{1}=L^{a_{m}}, Lj+1=LajL_{j+1}=L^{a_{j}}, 1≤j<r1\leq j<r, A=LA=L. Apply Theorem 1.2 to these line bundles, we obtain the exponent

deg(c1(Lam)∏j=1r−1c1(Laj)c1(L)n−r∩[X])=degLX⋅ama1⋯ar−1,\deg\left(c_{1}(L^{a_{m}})\prod_{j=1}^{r-1}c_{1}(L^{a_{j}})c_{1}(L)^{n-r}\cap[X]\right)=\deg_{L}X\cdot a_{m}a_{1}\cdots a_{r-1},

as required. ∎

Remark 4.1.

For Corollary 1.5, it suffices that the difference powers Laj−aiL^{a_{j}-a_{i}} appearing in (4.1) are globally generated. In particular, if n=1n=1 or m≤2m\leq 2, so LL only needs to be ample.

The proof of Corollary 1.5 uses global generation of the difference powers to choose its triangular sections. For ample line bundles, the following result gives bounds using a finite flat root cover and higher-degree auxiliary sections.

Corollary 4.2.

Let XX be an integral projective Cohen-Macaulay scheme of pure dimension n≥1n\geq 1 over a field kk. Let LL be an ample line bundle, and let fi∈H0​(X,Lai)f_{i}\in H^{0}(X,L^{a_{i}}) be nonzero sections with a1≥⋯≥am≥1a_{1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{m}\geq 1 that generate 𝒥\mathcal{J}. Then

(𝒥)degLX⋅a1⋯am⊆𝒥.(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{L}X\cdot a_{1}\cdots a_{m}}\subseteq\mathcal{J}.

If m>nm>n, choose b≥a1b\geq a_{1} such that Lb−aiL^{b-a_{i}} is globally generated for every i<mi<m. Then

(𝒥)degL⁡X⋅am​bn−1⊆𝒥.(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{L}X\cdot a_{m}b^{n-1}}\subseteq\mathcal{J}.

Thus the smaller of these two exponents is valid. In particular, the exponent of Corollary 1.5 remains valid for merely ample LL whenever m≤nm\leq n.

Proof.

Consider the finite flat cover π:Y→X\pi:Y\to X obtained by adjoining roots σiai=π∗​fi\sigma_{i}^{a_{i}}=\pi^{*}f_{i}. Its algebra is π∗​𝒪Y=⨂i=1m(⨁q=0ai−1L−q)\pi_{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}=\bigotimes_{i=1}^{m}\left(\bigoplus_{q=0}^{a_{i}-1}L^{-q}\right), with multiplication determined by the sections fif_{i}. The defining equations are successively monic in new variables, so they form a regular sequence over the local polynomial rings of XX. Thus YY is projective, Cohen-Macaulay and pure of dimension nn, and π∗​L\pi^{*}L is ample. Finite flatness and the projection formula give π∗[Y]=a1⋯am[X]\pi_{*}[Y]=a_{1}\cdots a_{m}[X], degπ∗​L(Y)=a1⋯amdegLX\deg_{\pi^{*}L}(Y)=a_{1}\cdots a_{m}\deg_{L}X, see [18, Tags 02RH and 02SU].

Let ℐ⊆𝒪Y\mathcal{I}\subseteq\mathcal{O}_{Y} be the ideal sheaf generated by the root sections σ1,…,σm\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{m}. Then ℐ⊗π∗​L\mathcal{I}\otimes\pi^{*}L is globally generated. Applying Corollary 1.3 with both ample line bundles taken to be π∗​L\pi^{*}L, we obtain (ℐ)degπ∗​L⁡(Y)⊆ℐ(\sqrt{\mathcal{I}})^{\deg_{\pi^{*}L}(Y)}\subseteq\mathcal{I}. Since 𝒥​𝒪Y⊆ℐ\mathcal{J}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{I}, it follows that (𝒥)degLXa1⋯am𝒪Y⊆ℐ(\sqrt{\mathcal{J}})^{\deg_{L}Xa_{1}\cdots a_{m}}\mathcal{O}_{Y}\subseteq\mathcal{I}.

The ideal ℐ\mathcal{I} contracts to 𝒥\mathcal{J}: locally, quotienting the root algebra by all the σi\sigma_{i} gives R/(f1,…,fm)R/(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}). This proves the first assertion.

For the second assertion, take s1=fms_{1}=f_{m}. It is regular because XX is integral. Remark 5.1.

Retain the assumptions and notation of Theorem 1.6, but remove the domain assumption on SS. The Cohen-Macaulay hypothesis still gives the weaker bound

Indeed, on X=Proj⁡S⁡[t]X=\operatorname{Proj}S[t], take 𝒥=I​S​[t]~\mathcal{J}=\widetilde{IS[t]}. We apply the triangular avoidance argument of Section 4 starting with degree a1a_{1}. This gives successive sections of degrees a1,…,amin⁡{m,n+1}a_{1},\ldots,a_{\min\{m,n+1\}} that are regular outside V⁡(𝒥)V(\mathcal{J}). If m<n+1m<n+1, these sections generate 𝒥\mathcal{J}, so the condition (2) of Theorem 1.2 also holds. Applying Theorem 1.2 with auxiliary line bundle 𝒪X​(1)\mathcal{O}_{X}(1) and restricting to D+​(t)≅Spec⁡SD_{+}(t)\cong\operatorname{Spec}S proves the assertion. However, this estimate does not, in general, recover the sharp exponent of [10, Theorem 1.5] for polynomial rings.

Remark 5.4.

The examples in parts (1) and (2) establish the sharpness of the containment bounds. These work over every field. In part (3), characteristic zero is used only to attain the additive bound for maxgi⁡(deg⁡gi+ai)\max_{g_{i}}(\deg g_{i}+a_{i}) by a power of a linear form. This characteristic-zero construction also shows that the uniform bound deg⁡gi+ai≤d\deg g_{i}+a_{i}\leq d cannot be improved in a statement valid over arbitrary fields. For δ=1\delta=1, the affine charts in the examples of part (3) are affine spaces, so these examples also establish sharpness for maxgi⁡deg⁡(gi​fi)\max_{g_{i}}\deg(g_{i}f_{i}).
